question: Online hate knows no borders, but the public response is still largely fragmented across Member States. France has an effective reporting tool – the PHAROS platform – managed by specialised services, while several other Member States, including Germany, Luxembourg, Portugal, the Netherlands and Ireland, have partial or comparable systems.

However, there is currently no EU mechanism to map and network those systems and to facilitate the crossborder exchange of reports, even though hateful content spreads instantly from one Member State to another.

Given the worrying resurgence in antisemitism and racist rhetoric online, it seems necessary to equip the EU with an operational coordination tool – CNORA, or the Coordination Network Against Online Racism and Antisemitism – that would supplement the framework laid down by the Digital Services Act. 1.

Can the Commission assess the legal, operational and budgetary conditions for such an EU coordination network, in particular under the Digital Services Act and the EU strategy on combating antisemitism?
What action will it take to encourage Member States that do not have a system equivalent to PHAROS to establish such a system?
How does it intend to ensure that those platforms are interoperable and that there is effective cooperation between them?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.10.2026) Antisemitism and racism are widespread online and can lead to radicalisation and physical attacks. Antisemitic or racist speech – both online and offline – that incites violence and hatred is criminalised under the Framework Decision on combating racism and xenophobia1.

However, for example on Holocaust denial and distortion, national laws still differ in many respects. The EU Strategy on Combating Antisemitism and Fostering Jewish Life (2021-2030)2 has set out targeted measures to strengthen the fight against online antisemitism, including by establishing network of organisations monitoring antisemitism online.
As part of the working group on the implementation of the strategy, Member States coordinate and share best practices.

While the Digital Services Act (DSA)3 does not contain provisions that would create a publicly available central online platform to notify illegal content, it creates clear obligations for all online platforms to instate user-friendly, accessible mechanisms for the flagging of suspected illegal content, and, if found to be illegal, the platform must act expeditiously to remove such content, or else risk facing liability.

The Code of conduct on countering illegal hate speech online +, integrated into the DSA framework and signed by major online platforms, seeks to prevent and address the spread of illegal hate speech online4. The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation coordinates action days targeting online racist and xenophobic hate speech and online terrorist and violent extremist content.

The High-level group on combating hate speech and hate crimes, set up by the Commission, aims to develop practical guidance, standards and tools, support capacity building and exchange good practices5.
